About

Cookies are pieces of data sent to your browser when you visit a website and are stored on your computer’s or mobile device’s hard drive. Cookies may store your preferences and other information but cannot read data off your hard disk or read cookie files created by other sites. 

You can at any time change or withdraw your consent on our website. Please review our entire Cookie Statement for more information. Learn more about who we are, how you can contact us and how we process personal data in our Privacy Policy.

Scientists Report Continuing Harms to U.S. Science in Second-Year Survey

September 21, 2026 Science Policy and Outreach, The Entomology Profession 1
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:45
Instaread

For a second year, a survey of nearly 1,000 scientists across a variety of life sciences details how recent federal government policies have created ongoing disruptions to American research and to the scientific workforce.

Scientists report negative impacts that are varied and far-reaching: curtailed research programs, loss of funding and jobs, restrictions on free speech, barriers to working with international collaborators, severe delays in funding decisions, and a general decline in government efficiency.

The survey gathered input from scientists—including members of the Entomological Society of America—across all career stages and sectors, including academia, federal government, nonprofit organizations, and industry, with respondents geographically distributed throughout the United States.

Key Findings

Data points of note from the survey responses include:

  • 79.7% of respondents said that federal policies since January 20, 2025, had caused an “extremely negative impact” (54.2%) or “irreparable harm” (25.5%) on their field of science.
  • 56% of respondents said the waiting time for decisions on federal grant proposals after January 20, 2025, has increased by “several months” compared to the two-year period before that time. Another 18% said the wait time has increase by “several weeks.”
  • Large portions of respondents reported that federal policies caused uncertainty about the future (78%) and increased stress and anxiety (75%).
  • 69% of respondents said that U.S. federal training programs were “very important” or “extremely important” to their development as scientists.

Scientists’ comments about the impacts highlighted several major concerns:

Funding cuts. Between grant cancellations and ensuing university budget cuts, respondents reported job losses, difficulty in securing roles for student researchers, discontinuation of research projects, and reduced institutional knowledge and expertise when long-time researchers left or were terminated.

Delays and uncertainty. Respondents shared stories of greatly slowed-down grant review timelines, frequent changes to funding opportunities, sudden program cancellations, and unresponsive agencies—all contributing to decreases in efficiency and increases of wasted time and effort for the scientists trying to conduct research while navigating administrative upheaval.

Research harms. Ongoing research programs have been interrupted or cancelled, leading to gaps in data sets or the outright disappearance of previously available data, respondents said. A number of respondents pointed to programs focused on disease and expressed concerns about resulting negative impacts on human health.

International barriers. Scientists reported that it is now harder to establish collaborations with researchers in foreign countries due to new restrictions on federally funded projects. They also said that it is harder to attract talented researchers from other countries to roles in U.S. institutions, due either directly to new restrictions on immigration or indirectly to fear among foreign researchers that they would be targeted with increased government surveillance or scrutiny in the U.S.

Censorship. Respondents reported new and increased policing of language and subjects prohibited from being included in grant proposals, research programs, teaching curricula, and more—all of which hinders their ability to pursue legitimate scientific questions and research priorities.

The State of American Science

The 2026 survey’s findings echo and expand upon the findings from 2025, and it reveals the continuation of significant damage to the U.S. research enterprise and its place in the American economy and society.

Moreover, the survey was conducted in June, mostly before researchers had become aware or fully understood the implications of proposed rule changes by the Office of Management and Budget for federal grants. The proposed changes are far-reaching and, if enacted, stand to significantly worsen the negative impacts already being felt by U.S. scientists.

The Entomological Society of America has joined numerous other scientific organizations in voicing opposition to OMB’s proposals and encourages its members to do the same via messages to their Congressional legislators. You can also join ESA or donate to support its mission to advocate for insect science.

March 5, 2021 Research News 0

A survey of soybean farmers finds misunderstandings about terms such as “economic threshold” and “economic injury level.” The results suggest that improved and well-tailored communication efforts could improve adoption of integrated pest management principles. [Read more]

  1. Steven Hammer says:
    September 21, 2026 at 5:03 pm

    This is the third article along these lines from Entomology Today. It continues to surprise me how scientists are excellent in their fields yet fail to understand the economic situation of our country. We have unfunded liabilities for Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security in excess of 70 trillion dollars. We have a national debt which is growing unchecked. Our government pays an ever increasing amount of the federal budget simply to pay the interest on our debt. This is not sustainable.

    Science does not exist apart from the greater economic situation of our country. The fact that there is some effort on the part of our nation’s leaders to reign in costs (admittedly unusual behavior for politicians) should be seen as normal and necessary given the economic reality of our country. No one likes tightening the budget. The field of medicine has been squeezed for years. It would be wonderful if there were unlimited dollars for every need, but that isn’t reality. It isn’t only entomology that feels the cuts.
